# A map of the bacteria

> *Lectures and textbooks name bacteria by group: Gram-positive cocci, Enterobacterales, anaerobes,
> spiral bacteria, atypicals. It can feel like a long list to memorise. This chapter shows that each
> group is a **combination of a few traits** you already know from the previous chapter, and that the
> combination explains how the group behaves.*

## Same questions, different answers {#sec-map-idea}

The previous chapter gave you a trait toolkit: envelope, shape, relationship with oxygen and growth.
This chapter adds two traits that matter for whole groups of bacteria:

- **Where it grows:** outside cells, able to live inside cells, or *only* inside cells.
- **What it needs to grow in the lab:** ordinary media, enriched media, weeks of time, or living cells.

A bacterial group is then a short description in those terms. *Enterobacterales*, for example, are
"Gram-negative rods that cope with or without oxygen, ferment sugars, and live in the gut". Once you
can read a group that way, its name stops being a label to memorise and becomes a summary of how it
lives.

Groups are named in different ways, which is part of what makes the list confusing. Some names are
family trees (*Enterobacterales*). Some describe one trait (anaerobes, spiral bacteria). Some describe
a failure of the usual methods ("fastidious", "atypical"). The map puts them all on the same footing.

## Metabolism predicts habitat {#sec-habitat}

Two groups on the map are both Gram-negative rods, yet one lives in your gut and the other in water
and soil. The difference is how they make ATP. Find it below.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-ecoli-pseudomonas.yml"></div>

The same reasoning explains the **fastidious** bacteria. Over evolutionary time, a bacterium that
lives on a rich host can lose genes for making nutrients the host already supplies. It then depends on
finding them. *Haemophilus*, for example, needs two factors found inside red blood cells, so the lab
grows it on agar made with blood that has been heated until the cells burst: **chocolate agar**, named
for its brown colour. "Fastidious" is a description of lost biosynthesis, not of difficulty for its own
sake.

::: {.callout-note}
## Bridge from the previous chapter
**Gram-negative cocci** (*Neisseria*) show the same logic from another angle. They live only in
humans and die quickly outside the body: they dry out, and they need enriched media in the lab. A
fragile organism can only spread by close contact between people, which is exactly how the two main
*Neisseria* species spread.
:::

## Worked example: why "atypical"? {#sec-atypicals}

The **atypicals** are three genera, *Mycoplasma*, *Chlamydia* and *Rickettsia*, that are not closely
related. They are grouped because the usual microbiology toolkit fails on them. The name comes from
the clinic: the chest infections some of them cause did not look like typical bacterial pneumonia,
and did not respond to penicillin.

The useful question is not "what are the atypicals?" but **"why does the toolkit fail?"** There are
two different reasons, and each predicts a lot.

| | *Mycoplasma* | *Chlamydia* | *Rickettsia* |
|---|---|---|---|
| What is unusual | **No cell wall at all** | **Lives only inside host cells**; two-form life cycle | **Lives only inside host cells**, free in the cytoplasm |
| Envelope | Membrane only, stiffened with sterols | Gram-negative-type, with very little peptidoglycan | Gram-negative-type |
| Energy | Makes its own ATP | Imports ATP from the host cell | Imports ATP from the host cell |
| How it spreads | Respiratory droplets | Direct contact (sexual, or eye to eye) | Bites of ticks, lice, fleas or mites |
| Gram stain | Nothing to read | Too small, and hidden inside cells | Stains poorly |
| Lab growth | Slowly, on media enriched with sterols | Only in living cells | Only in living cells |

Start with the first reason, a missing wall. Predict what follows from it.

<div data-island="microbe-profile" data-src="/diagrams/profile-m-pneumoniae.yml"></div>

Now the second reason. *Chlamydia* also fails the Gram stain and will not grow on agar, but for a
different cause.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-mycoplasma-chlamydia.yml"></div>

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "atypical means rare or unimportant"
"Atypical" describes the toolkit, not how often these bacteria cause disease. *Chlamydia trachomatis*
is one of the most common sexually transmitted bacteria in the world, and *Mycoplasma pneumoniae* is a
common cause of chest infection in children and young adults. They are atypical only in the sense that
standard stains and cultures miss them, which is why labs usually detect them by their DNA.
:::

**What the organ-system blocks will add.** In the respiratory, genitourinary and infection blocks you
will meet each of these organisms again, with the diseases they cause, how they are diagnosed and how
they are treated. You will not need to memorise those facts as a separate list. Each one follows from
two ideas on this page: *no wall*, or *lives only inside cells*.
